entries.9417a5964e4b1d67e1695f704966cb75997f47bf: <chapter n="99" osisID="Ps.99" sID="Ps.99"/> <div sID="gen12267" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12268" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12269" type="x-p"/> Still we are celebrating the glories of the kingdom of God among men, and are called upon to praise him, as in the foregoing psalms; but those psalms looked forward to the times of the gospel, and prophesied of the graces and comforts of those times; this psalm seems to dwell more upon the Old-Testament dispensation and the manifestation of God's glory and grace in that. The Jews were not, in expectation of the Messiah's kingdom and the evangelical worship, to neglect the divine regimen they were then under, and the ordinances that were then given them, but in them to see God reigning, and to worship before him according to the law of Moses. Prophecies of good things to come must not lessen our esteem of good things present. To Israel indeed pertained the promises, which they were bound to believe; but to them pertained also the giving of the law, and the service of God, which they were also bound dutifully and conscientiously to attend to, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>. And this they are called to do in this psalm, where yet there is much of Christ, for the government of the church was in the hands of the eternal Word before he was incarnate; and, besides, the ceremonial services were types and figures of evangelical worship. The people of Israel are here required to praise and exalt God, and to worship before him, in consideration of these two things:—I. The happy constitution of the government they were under, both in sacred and civil things, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Some instances of the happy administration of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.6-Ps.99.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. In singing this psalm we must set ourselves to exalt the name of God, as it is made known to us in the gospel, which we have much more reason to do than those had who lived under the law.
entries.5655c360139c11f80d0e79f65557f91e06b67d91: <div eID="gen12269" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12268" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Dominion of God.</title> <div sID="gen12270" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> reigneth; let the people tremble: he sitteth <hi type="italic">between</hi> the cherubims; let the earth be moved. <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> great in Zion; and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> high above all the people. <hi type="super">3</hi> Let them praise thy great and terrible name; <hi type="italic">for</hi> it <hi type="italic">is</hi> holy. <hi type="super">4</hi> The king's strength also loveth judgment; thou dost establish equity, thou executest judgment and righteousness in Jacob. <hi type="super">5</hi> Exalt ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, and worship at his footstool; <hi type="italic">for</hi> he <hi type="italic">is</hi> holy. <div eID="gen12270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12271" type="x-p"/> The foundation of all religion is laid in this truth, That <hi type="italic">the Lord reigns.</hi> God governs the world by his providence, governs the church by his grace, and both by his Son. We are to believe not only that <hi type="italic">the Lord lives,</hi> but that <hi type="italic">the Lord reigns.</hi> This is the triumph of the Christian church, and here it was the triumph of the Jewish church, that Jehovah was their King; and hence it is inferred, <hi type="italic">Let the people tremble,</hi> that is, 1. Let even the subjects of this kingdom tremble; for the Old-Testament dispensation had much of terror in it. At Mount Sinai Israel, and even Moses himself, did <hi type="italic">exceedingly fear and quake;</hi> and then God was <hi type="italic">terrible in his holy places.</hi> Even when he appeared in his people's behalf, he did terrible things. But we are not now come to <hi type="italic">that mount that burned with fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>. Now that <hi type="italic">the Lord reigns let the earth rejoice.</hi> Then he ruled more by the power of holy fear; now he rules by the power of holy love. 2. Much more let the enemies of this kingdom tremble; for he will either bring them into obedience to his golden sceptre or crush them with his iron rod. <hi type="italic">The Lord reigns, though the people be stirred with indignation</hi> at it; though they fret away all their spirits, their rage is all in vain. He will set his King upon his holy hill of Zion in spite of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 1-6</reference>); first, or last, he will make them <hi type="italic">tremble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">The Lord reigns, let the earth be moved.</hi> Those that submit to him shall be established, and not <hi type="italic">moved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Ps. xcvi. 10</reference>); but those that oppose him will be moved. Heaven and earth shall be shaken, and all nations; but the kingdom of Christ is what cannot be moved; the <hi type="italic">things which cannot be shaken shall remain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">Heb. xii. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">In these is continuance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa. lxiv. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen12271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12272" type="x-p"/> God's kingdom, set up in Israel, is here made the subject of the psalmist's praise. <div eID="gen12272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12273" type="x-p"/> I. Two things the psalmist affirms:—1. God presided in the affairs of religion: <hi type="italic">He sitteth between the cherubim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.1">v. 1</reference>), as on his throne, to give law by the oracles thence delivered—as on the mercy-seat, to receive petitions. This was the honour of Israel, that they had among them the Shechinah, or special presence of God, attended by the holy angels; the temple was the royal palace, and the Holy of holies was the presence-chamber. <hi type="italic">The Lord is great in Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.2">v. 2</reference>); there he is known and praised (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.2">Ps. lxxvi. 1, 2</reference>); there he is served as great, more than any where else. <hi type="italic">He is high</hi> there <hi type="italic">above all people;</hi> as that which is high is exposed to view, and looked up to, so in Zion the perfections of the divine nature appear more conspicuous and more illustrious than any where else. Therefore <hi type="italic">let those</hi> that dwell in Zion, and worship there, <hi type="italic">praise thy great and terrible name,</hi> and give thee the glory due unto it, <hi type="italic">for it is holy.</hi> The holiness of God's name makes it truly great to his friends and terrible to his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.3">v. 3</reference>. This is that which those above adore—<hi type="italic">Holy, holy, holy.</hi> 2. He was all in all in their civil government, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.4">v. 4</reference>. As in Jerusalem was the testimony of Israel, whither the tribes went up, so <hi type="italic">there were set thrones of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.122.4-Ps.122.5">Ps. cxxii. 4, 5</reference>. Their government was a theocracy. God raised up David to rule over them (and some think this psalm was penned upon occasion of his quiet and happy settlement in the throne) and he is <hi type="italic">the king</hi> whose <hi type="italic">strength loves judgment.</hi> He is strong; all his strength he has from God; and <hi type="italic">his strength</hi> is not abused for the support of any wrong, as the power of great princes often is, but it <hi type="italic">loves judgment.</hi> He does justice with his power, and does it with delight; and herein he was a type of Christ, to whom God would give <hi type="italic">the throne of his father David, to do judgment and justice.</hi> He has power to crush, but his <hi type="italic">strength loves judgment;</hi> he does not rule with rigour, but with moderation, with wisdom, and with tenderness. The people of Israel had a good king; but they are here taught to look up to God as he by whom their king reigns: <hi type="italic">Thou dost establish equity</hi> (that is, God gave them those excellent laws by which they were governed), and <hi type="italic">thou executest judgment and righteousness in Jacob;</hi> he not only by his immediate providences often executed and enforced his own laws, but took care for the administration of justice among them by civil magistrates, who reigned by him and by him did decree justice. Their judges judged for God, and their judgment was his, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.6">2 Chron. xix. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen12273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12274" type="x-p"/> II. Putting these two things together, we see what was the happiness of Israel above any other people, as Moses had described it (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.7-Deut.4.8">Deut. iv. 7, 8</reference>), that they had <hi type="italic">God so nigh unto them,</hi> sitting between the cherubim, and that they had <hi type="italic">statutes and judgments so righteous,</hi> by which equity was established, and God himself ruled in Jacob, from which he infers this command to that happy people (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Exalt you the Lord our God, and worship at his footstool;</hi> give him the glory of the good government you are under, as it is now established, both in church and state." Note, 1. The greater the public mercies are which we have a share in the more we are obliged to bear a part in the public homage paid to God: the setting up of the kingdom of Christ, especially, ought to be the matter of our praise. 2. When we draw night to God, to worship him, our hearts must be filled with high thoughts of him, and he must be exalted in our souls. 3. The more we abase ourselves, and the more prostrate we are before God, the more we exalt him. We must <hi type="italic">worship at his footstool,</hi> at his ark, which was as the footstool to the mercy-seat between the cherubim; or we must cast ourselves down upon the pavement of his courts; and good reason we have to be thus reverent, <hi type="italic">for he is holy,</hi> and his holiness should strike an awe upon us, as it does on the angels themselves, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.2-Isa.6.3">Isa. vi. 2, 3</reference>.
entries.25037bec917cdedf184de7ca298bbef801eb487f: <div eID="gen12274" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Justice and Mercy.</title> <div sID="gen12275" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name; they called upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he answered them. <hi type="super">7</hi> He spake unto them in the cloudy pillar: they kept his testimonies, and the ordinance <hi type="italic">that</hi> he gave them. <hi type="super">8</hi> Thou answeredst them, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions. <hi type="super">9</hi> Exalt the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, and worship at his holy hill; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> holy. <div eID="gen12275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12276" type="x-p"/> The happiness of Israel in God's government is here further made out by some particular instances of his administration, especially with reference to those that were, in their day, the prime leaders and most active useful governors of that people—Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, in the two former of whom the theocracy or divine government began (for they were employed to form Israel into a people) and in the last of whom that form of government, in a great measure, ended; for when the people rejected Samuel, and urged him to resign, they are said to reject God himself, that he should not be so immediately their king as he had been (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.7">1 Sam. viii. 7</reference>), for now they would have a king, like all the nations. Moses, as well as Aaron, is said to be <hi type="italic">among his priests,</hi> for he executed the priest's office till Aaron was settled in it and he consecrated Aaron and his sons; therefore the Jews call him the <hi type="italic">priest of the priests.</hi> Now concerning these three chief rulers observe, <div eID="gen12276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12277" type="x-p"/> I. The intimate communion they had with God, and the wonderful favour to which he admitted them. None of all the nations of the earth could produce three such men as these, that had such an intercourse with Heaven, and whom God <hi type="italic">knew by name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.33.17">Exod. xxxiii. 17</reference>. Here is, 1. Their gracious observance of God. No kingdom had men that honoured God as these three men of the kingdom of Israel did. They honoured him, (1.) By their prayers. Samuel, though not among his priests, yet was <hi type="italic">among those that called on his name;</hi> and for <hi type="italic">this</hi> they were all famous, <hi type="italic">They called upon the Lord;</hi> they relied not on their own wisdom or virtue, but in every emergency had recourse to God, towards him was their desire, and on him their dependence. (2.) By their obedience: <hi type="italic">They kept his testimonies, and the ordinances that he gave them;</hi> they made conscience of their duty, and in every thing made God's word and law their rule, as knowing that unless they did so they could not expect their prayers should be answered, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Prov. xxviii. 9</reference>. Moses did all according to the pattern shown him; it is often repeated, <hi type="italic">According to all that God commanded Moses, so did he.</hi> Aaron and Samuel did likewise. Those were the greatest men and most honourable that were most eminent for keeping God's testimonies and conforming to the rule of his word. 2. God's gracious acceptance of them: <hi type="italic">He answered them,</hi> and granted them the things which they called upon him for. They all wonderfully prevailed with God in prayer; miracles were wrought at their special instance and request; nay, he not only condescended to do that for them which they desired, as a prince for a petitioner, but he communed with them as one friend familiarly converses with another (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">He spoke unto them in the cloudy pillar.</hi> He often spoke to Samuel; from his childhood the word of the Lord came to him, and, probably, sometimes he spoke to him by a bright cloud overshadowing him: however, to Moses and Aaron he often spoke out of the famous <hi type="italic">cloudy pillar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.16.10">Exod. xvi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.5">Num. xii. 5</reference>. Israel are now reminded of this, for the confirming of their faith, that though they had not every day such sensible tokens of God's presence as the cloudy pillar was, yet to those that were their first founders, and to him that was their great reformer, God was pleased thus to manifest himself. <div eID="gen12277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12278" type="x-p"/> II. The good offices they did to Israel. They interceded for the people, and for them also they obtained many an answer of peace. <hi type="italic">Moses stood in the gap,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Aaron between the living and the dead;</hi> and, when Israel was in distress, Samuel cried unto the Lord for them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.9">1 Sam. vii. 9</reference>. This is here referred to (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou answeredst them, O Lord our God!</hi> and, at their prayer, <hi type="italic">thou wast a God that forgavest</hi> the people they prayed for; and, <hi type="italic">though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions,</hi> yet thou didst not cut them off from being a people, as their sin deserved." "<hi type="italic">Thou wast a God that wast propitious for them</hi> (so Dr. Hammond), for their sakes, and sparedst the people at their request, even when thou wast about to <hi type="italic">take vengeance of their inventions,</hi> that is, when thy wrath was so highly provoked against them that it was just ready to break in upon them, to their utter overthrow." These were some of the many remarkable instances of God's dominion in Israel, more than in any other nation, for which the people are again called upon to praise God (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Exalt the Lord our God,</hi> on account of what he has done for us formerly, as well as of late, <hi type="italic">and worship at his holy hill</hi> of Zion, on which he has now set his temple and will shortly <hi type="italic">set his King</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>), the former a type of the latter; there, as the centre of unity, let all God's Israel meet, with their adorations, <hi type="italic">for the Lord our God is holy,</hi> and appears so, not only in his holy law, but in his holy gospel."  <chapter eID="Ps.99"/> <div eID="gen12278" type="x-p"/>

entries.51a3b08c8a3b63a293ef0915a3f312e930bbc0e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6637"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 99</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.9">Psa 99:1-9</reference>. God's government is especially exercised in and for His Church, which should praise Him for His gracious dealings.</title> <div sID="gen10162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6637"/><hi type="bold">1. sitteth ... cherubim--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.4">1Sa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Psa 80:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tremble ... be moved--</hi>inspired with fear by His judgments on the wicked. <div eID="gen10163" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdecfadfe4e5a5718e1a7d7e23a052d830a212dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6638"/><div sID="gen10164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6638"/><hi type="bold">2. great in Zion--</hi>where He dwells (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.11">Psa 9:11</reference>). <div eID="gen10164" type="x-p"/>
entries.838e49ceabf62ca73db76c9c309166d5663c237f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6639"/><div sID="gen10165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6639"/><hi type="bold">3. thy ... name--</hi>perfections of justice, power, &c.<div eID="gen10165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great and terrible name--</hi>producing dread (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">De 10:17</reference>), and to be praised by those over whom He is exalted (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">Psa 97:9</reference>).<div eID="gen10166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is holy--</hi>or, "He is holy" (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Psa 99:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10167" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a52b87b23cae7ae76eddf07324de6c736791a41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6640"/><div sID="gen10168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6640"/>4-5. To His wise and righteous government all nations should render honor.<div eID="gen10168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king's ... judgment--</hi>His power is combined with justice.<div eID="gen10169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is holy--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.3">Psa 22:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10170" type="x-p"/>
entries.714b439ef8ffaddc14a05eb92623b1b52781680c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6641"/><div sID="gen10171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6641"/>6-8. The experience of these servants of God is cited for encouragement.<div eID="gen10171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among ... priests, among ... upon the Lord [and] He spake ... pillar--</hi>may be referred to all three (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.18.19">Ex 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.8.15">Le 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.5">De 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13">1Sa 9:13</reference>). <div eID="gen10172" type="x-p"/>

entries.1e0e9770f5c646c41fa1c9929375e31e096c127f: <div eID="gen21891" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21892" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21893" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21893" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21892" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21894" type="x-p"/> The empire of God in the world and the Church, <reference osisRef="Psa.99.1">Psa 99:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.99.2">Psa 99:2</reference>. He ought to be praised, <reference osisRef="Psa.99.3">Psa 99:3</reference>. Justice and judgment are his chief glory, <reference osisRef="Psa.99.4">Psa 99:4</reference>. He should be worshipped as among the saints of old, whom he graciously answered and saved, <reference osisRef="Psa.99.5-Psa.99.8">Psa 99:5-8</reference>. Exalt him because he is holy, <reference osisRef="Psa.99.9">Psa 99:9</reference>. <div eID="gen21894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21895" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew and Chaldee have no title; all the versions but the Chaldee attribute it to David. The Syriac says it concerns "the slaughter of the Midianites which Moses and the children of Israel had taken captive; and is a prophecy concerning the glory of the kingdom of Christ." But the mention of Samuel shows that it cannot be referred to the time of Moses. Calmet thinks that it was sung at the dedication of the city, or of the second temple, after the return from the Babylonish captivity. Eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. join it to the preceding psalm. <div eID="gen21895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21896" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21897" type="x-p"/> The Lord reigneth - See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.97.1">Psa 97:1</reference>. <div eID="gen21897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21898" type="x-p"/> Let the people tremble - He will establish his kingdom in spite of his enemies; let those who oppose him tremble for the consequences. <div eID="gen21898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21899" type="x-p"/> He sitteth between the cherubims - This is in reference to the ark, at each end of which was a cherub of glory; and the shechinah, or symbol of the Divine Presence, appeared on the lid of the ark, called also the mercy-seat, between the cherubim. Sitting between the cherubim implies God's graciousness and mercy. While then, in his reign, he was terrible to sinners, he is on the throne of grace to all who fear love, and obey him. Though this symbol were not in the second temple, yet the Divine Being might very well be thus denominated, because it had become one of his titles, he having thus appeared under the tabernacle and first temple.
entries.28aabc877f2dcf7ced7a65d62d2f55f7d6d13836: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21900" type="x-p"/> The Lord is great in Zion - It is among his own worshippers that he has manifested his power and glory in an especial manner. There he is known, and there he is worthily magnified.
entries.aa3645aa10cc0f181dc2f492f843ef18698f688d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21901" type="x-p"/> Let them praise thy great and terrible name - Let them confess thee to be great and terrible: let them tremble before thee. <div eID="gen21901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21902" type="x-p"/> For it is holy - קדוש הוא kadosh hu. As this not only ends this verse but the fifth also, and in effect the ninth, it seems to be a species of chorus which was sung in a very solemn manner at the conclusion of each of these parts. His holiness - the immaculate purity of his nature, was the reason why he should be exalted, praised, and worshipped.
entries.ffc0b9879916810b3098fcb5efdf3ba37065149c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21903" type="x-p"/> The king's strength - If this Psalm were written by David, he must mean by it that he was God's vicegerent or deputy, and that, even as king, God was his strength, and the pattern according to which equity, judgment, and righteousness should be executed in Jacob.
entries.91774c55a46d5aec588570ca1261b96acb41e28a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21904" type="x-p"/> Worship at his footstool - Probably meaning the ark on which the Divine glory was manifested. Sometimes the earth is called God's footstool, <reference osisRef="Mat.5.35">Mat 5:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Isa 66:1</reference>; sometimes Jerusalem; sometimes the temple, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">Lam 2:1</reference>; sometimes the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.7">Psa 32:7</reference>; and sometimes the ark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Chr 28:2</reference>. The Israelites, when they worshipped, turned their faces toward the ark, because that was the place where was the symbol of the Divine Presence. <div eID="gen21904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21905" type="x-p"/> For he is holy - The burden chanted by the chorus.
entries.20685896725b590165e4615a4dfe155a4cdb1ef7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21906" type="x-p"/> Moses and Aaron - As Moses and Aaron among the priests, and as Samuel among the prophets, worshipped God in humility, gratitude, and the spirit of obedience, and received the strongest tokens of the Divine favor; so worship ye the Lord, that he may bless, support, and save you. Moses was properly the priest of the Hebrews before Aaron and his family were appointed to that office.
entries.800b79547b2b214481a6ff67913e48b93b5a2cef: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21907" type="x-p"/> He spake unto them in the cloudy pillar - That is, he directed all their operations, marchings, and encampments by this cloudy pillar. See <reference osisRef="Exo.33.9">Exo 33:9</reference>. <div eID="gen21907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21908" type="x-p"/> They kept his testimonies - Do ye the same, and God will be your portion as he was theirs.
entries.45040da921645e40b98452f46d062ff592e9b3dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21909" type="x-p"/> Thou - forgavest them - When the people had sinned, and wrath was about to descend on them, Moses and Aaron interceded for them, and they were not destroyed. <div eID="gen21909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21910" type="x-p"/> Tookest vengeance of their inventions - God spared them, but showed his displeasure at their misdoings. He chastised, but did not consume them. This is amply proved in the history of this people.
entries.48b62ab64e67dcc38cc185e86316ee781a2a4e29: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21911" type="x-p"/> Worship at his holy hill - Worship him publicly in the temple. <div eID="gen21911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21912" type="x-p"/> For the Lord our God is holy - The words of the chorus; as in the third and fifth verses.  <chapter eID="Ps.99"/> <div eID="gen21912" type="x-p"/>

entries.d4bc43f8997102158d58c6768a38a6846339a263: <div eID="gen9961" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Song of Praise in Honour of the Thrice Holy One</title> <div sID="gen9962" type="x-p"/> This is the third of the Psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:1-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.97.1-Ps.97.12">Psa 97:1-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.9">Psa 99:1-9</reference>) which begin with the watchword מלך ה. It falls into three parts, of which the first (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.3">Psa 99:1-3</reference>) closes with קדושׁ הוּא, the second (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.4">Psa 99:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Psa 99:5</reference>) with קדושׁ הוּא, and the third, more full-toned, with אלחנוּ קדושׁ ה - an earthly echo of the trisagion of the seraphim. The first two Sanctuses are two hexastichs; and two hexastichs form the third, according to the very same law by which the third and the sixth days of creation each consists of two creative works. This artistic form bears witness against Olshausen in favour of the integrity of the text; but the clare-obscure of the language and expression makes no small demands upon the reader. <div eID="gen9962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9963" type="x-p"/> Bengel has seen deepest into the internal character of this Psalm. He says, “The 99th Psalm has three parts, in which the Lord is celebrated as He who is to come, as He who is, and as He who was, and each part is closed with the ascription of praise: He is holy.” The Psalm is laid out accordingly by Oettinger, Burk, and C. H. Rieger.
entries.ded9a78b855493f8f1efcb65e42f7936b45f889f: <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.3">Psa 99:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9964" type="x-p"/> The three futures express facts of the time to come, which are the inevitable result of Jahve’s kingly dominion bearing sway from heaven, and here below from Zion, over the world; they therefore declare what must and will happen. The participle <hi type="italic">insidens cherubis</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Psa 80:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>) is a definition of the manner (Olshausen): He reigns, sitting enthroned above the cherubim. נוּט, like Arab. <hi type="italic">nwd</hi>, is a further formation of the root <hi type="italic">na</hi>, nu, to bend, nod. What is meant is not a trembling that is the absolute opposite of joy, but a trembling that leads on to salvation. The <hi type="italic">Breviarium in Psalterium</hi>, which bears the name of Jerome, observes: <hi type="italic">Terra quamdiu immota fuerit, sanari non potest; quando vero mota fuerit et intremuerit, tunc recipiet sanitatem.</hi> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.3">Psa 99:3</reference></hi> declaration passes over into invocation. One can feel how the hope that the “great and fearful Name” (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">Deu 10:17</reference>) will be universally acknowledged, and therefore that the religion of Israel will become the religion of the world, moves and elates the poet. The fact that the expression notwithstanding is not קדושׁ אתּה, but קדושׁ הוּא, is explained from the close connection with the seraphic trisagion in Isa 6:3. הוּא refers to Jahve; He and His Name are notions that easily glide over into one another.
entries.808eefe2d81e055d2202ff35bb552ee6b4cd8f0e: <reference osisRef="Ps.99.4-Ps.99.5">Psa 99:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen9964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9965" type="x-p"/> The second <hi type="italic">Sanctus</hi> celebrates Jahve with respect to His continuous righteous rule in Israel. The majority of expositors construe it: “And (they shall praise) the might of the king, who loves right;” but this joining of the clause on to יודוּ over the refrain that stands in the way is hazardous. Neither can ועז מלך משׁפּט אהב, however, be an independent clause, since אהב cannot be said of עז, but only of its possessor. And the dividing of the verse at אהב, adopted by the lxx, will therefore not hold good. משפט אהב is an attributive clause to מלך in the same position as in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.7">Psa 11:7</reference>; and עז, with what appertains to it, is the object to כּוננתּ placed first, which has the king’s throne as its object elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.8">Psa 9:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.13">2Sa 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.12">1Ch 17:12</reference>), just as it here has the might of the king, which, however, here at the same time in מישׁרים takes another and permutative object (cf. the permutative subject in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Psa 72:17</reference>), as Hitzig observes; or rather, since מישׁרים is most generally used as an adverbial notion, this מישׁרים (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Psa 75:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>, and frequently), usually as a definition of the mode of the judging and reigning, is subordinated: and the might of a king who loves the right, i.e., of one who governs not according to dynastic caprice but moral precepts, hast Thou established in spirit and aim (directed to righteousness and equity). What is meant is the theocratic kingship, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference> </hi>says what Jahve has constantly accomplished by means of this kingship: He has thus maintained right and righteousness (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2Sa 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.14">1Ch 18:14</reference>; 1Ki 10:9; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Isa 16:5</reference>) among His people. Out of this manifestation of God’s righteousness, which is more conspicuous, and can be better estimated, within the nation of the history of redemption than elsewhere, grows the call to highly exalt Jahve the God of Israel, and to bow one’s self very low at His footstool. להדם רגליו, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.7">Psa 132:7</reference>, is not a statement of the object (for <reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Isa 45:14</reference> is of another kind), but (like אל in other instances) of the place in which, or of the direction (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14">Psa 7:14</reference>) in which the προσκύνησις is to take place. The temple is called Jahve’s footstool (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">Lam 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.13">Isa 60:13</reference>) with reference to the ark, the <hi type="italic">capporeth</hi> of which corresponds to the transparent sapphire (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Exo 24:10</reference>) and to the crystal-like firmament of the <hi type="italic">mercaba</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.22">Eze 1:22</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.18">1Ch 28:18</reference>).
entries.0034f664e06b8ab5ed933a155316d96b6ac2e65e: <reference osisRef="Ps.99.6-Ps.99.9">Psa 99:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen9965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9966" type="x-p"/> The vision of the third <hi type="italic">Sanctus</hi> looks into the history of the olden time prior to the kings. In support of the statement that Jahve is a living God, and a God who proves Himself in mercy and in judgment, the poet appeals to three heroes of the olden time, and the events recorded of them. The expression certainly sounds as though it had reference to something belonging to the present time; and Hitzig therefore believes that it must be explained of the three as heavenly intercessors, after the manner of Onias and Jeremiah in the vision 2 Macc. 15:12-14. But apart from this presupposing an active manifestation of life on the part of those who have fallen happily asleep, which is at variance with the ideas of the latest as well as of the earliest Psalms concerning the other world, this interpretation founders upon <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.7">Psa 99:7</reference></hi>, according to which a celestial discourse of God with the three “in the pillar of cloud” ought also to be supposed. The substantival clauses <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference></hi> bear sufficient evident in themselves of being a retrospect, by which the futures that follow are stamped as being the expression of the contemporaneous past. The distribution of the predicates to the three is well conceived. Moses was also a mighty man in prayer, for with his hands uplifted for prayer he obtained the victory for his people over Amalek (Exo 17:11.), and on another occasion placed himself in the breach, and rescued them from the wrath of God and from destruction (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Psa 106:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.30-Exod.32.32">Exo 32:30-32</reference>; cf. also Num 12:13); and Samuel, it is true, is only a Levite by descent, but by office in a time of urgent need a priest (<hi type="italic">cohen</hi>), for he sacrifices independently in places where, by reason of the absence of the holy tabernacle with the ark of the covenant, it was not lawful, according to the letter of the law, to offer sacrifices, he builds an altar in Ramah, his residence as judge, and has, in connection with the divine services on the high place (<hi type="italic">Bama</hi>) there, a more than high-priestly position, inasmuch as the people do not begin the sacrificial repasts before he has blessed the sacrifice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13">1Sa 9:13</reference>). But the character of a mighty man in prayer is outweighed in the case of Moses by the character of the priest; for he is, so to speak, the proto-priest of Israel, inasmuch as he twice performed priestly acts which laid as it were a foundation for all times to come, viz., the sprinkling of the blood at the ratification of the covenant under Sinai (Ex. 24), and the whole ritual which was a model for the consecrated priesthood, at the consecration of the priests (Lev. 8). It was he, too, who performed the service in the sanctuary prior to the consecration of the priests: he set the shew-bread in order, prepared the candlestick, and burnt incense upon the golden altar (<reference osisRef="Exod.40.22-Exod.40.27">Exo 40:22-27</reference>). In the case of Samuel, on the other hand, the character of the mediator in the religious services is outweighed by that of the man mighty in prayer: by prayer he obtained Israel the victory of Ebenezer over the Philistines (1Sa 7:8.), and confirmed his words of warning with the miraculous sign, that at his calling upon God it would thunder and rain in the midst of a cloudless season (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.16">1Sa 12:16</reference>, cf. Sir. 46:16f.). <div eID="gen9966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9967" type="x-p"/> The poet designedly says: Moses and Aaron were among His priests, and Samuel among His praying ones. This third twelve-line strophe holds good, not only of the three in particular, but of the twelve-tribe nation of priests and praying ones to which they belong. For <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.7">Psa 99:7</reference></hi> cannot be meant of the three, since, with the exception of a single instance (Num 12:5), it is always Moses only, not Aaron, much less Samuel, with whom God negotiates in such a manner. אליהם refers to the whole people, which is proved by their interest in the divine revelation given by the hand of Moses out of the cloudy pillar (Exo 33:7.). Nor can <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference></hi> therefore be understood of the three exclusively, since there is nothing to indicate the transition from them to the people: crying (קראים, syncopated like חטאים,    <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">1Sa 24:11</reference>) to Jahve, i.e., as often as they (these priests and praying ones, to whom a Moses, Aaron, and Samuel belong) cried unto Jahve, He answered them-He revealed Himself to this people who had such leaders (<hi type="italic">choragi</hi>), in the cloudy pillar, to those who kept His testimonies and the law which He gave them. A glance at <reference osisRef="Ps.99.8">Psa 99:8</reference> shows that in Israel itself the good and the bad, good and evil, are distinguished. God answered those who could pray to Him with a claim to be answered. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.99.7">Psa 99:7</reference></hi>, is, virtually at least, a relative clause, declaring the prerequisite of a prayer that may be granted. In <reference osisRef="Ps.99.8">Psa 99:8</reference> is added the thought that the history of Israel, in the time of its redemption out of Egypt, is not less a mirror of the righteousness of God than of the pardoning grace of God. If <reference osisRef="Ps.99.7-Ps.99.8">Psa 99:7-8</reference> are referred entirely to the three, then עלילות and נקם, referred to their sins of infirmity, appear to be too strong expressions. But to take the suffix of עלילותם objectively (<hi type="italic">ea quae in eos sunt moliti Core et socii ejus</hi>), with Symmachus (καὶ ἔκδικος ἐπὶ ταῖς ἐπηρείναις αὐτῶν) and Kimchi, as the <hi type="italic">ulciscens in omnes adinventiones eorum</hi> of the Vulgate is interpreted,<note placement="foot">Vid., Raemdonck in his <hi type="italic">David propheta cet.</hi> 1800: <hi type="italic">in omnes injurias ipsis illatas, uti patuit in Core cet</hi>.</note> is to do violence to it. The reference to the people explains it all without any constraint, and even the flight of prayer that comes in here (cf. Mic 7:18). The calling to mind of the generation of the desert, which fell short of the promise, is an earnest admonition for the generation of the present time. The God of Israel is holy in love and in wrath, as He Himself unfolds His Name in <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>-7. Hence the poet calls upon his fellow-countrymen to exalt this God, whom they may with pride call their own, i.e., to acknowledge and confess His majesty, and to fall down and worship at (ל cf. אל, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>) the mountain of His holiness, the place of His choice and of His presence.  <chapter eID="Ps.99"/> <div eID="gen9967" type="x-p"/>

entries.79e8bf7be70a8e086e54d0c18399cfd83f663484:
PSALM 99
This psalm differs from those which precede it in one respect, that it speaks of the kingdom of God, and the blessings consequent upon it, as confined within Judea; and rather calls upon the posterity of Abraham, in distinction from the surrounding nations, to praise God for the privilege of their adoption.
Psalm 99:1-4
1. Jehovah reigns; let the people tremble: he dwells between the cherubim; let the earth be moved. 2. Jehovah is great in Zion; and he is high above all nations. 3. They shall acknowledge thy great and terrible name; it is holy. 4. The king’s strength
“The king’s strength seems here put for the king himself.” — Merrick Street removes the original word for strength to the end of the preceding verse, reading holy and mighty; and renders the first part of this verse thus: “Thou art a king that lovest judgment;” observing, that, in the Hebrew it is מלך, melech, not המלך, hamelech, that the word אהב, aheb, that lovest, is a participle here, and that the pronoun אתה, atah, thou, belongs to the first clause. “According to the translation of the English Bible,” says he, “there is a great want of connection. ‘The king’s strength also loveth judgment: thou dost establish equity,’ etc. There had been no king spoken of before except Jehovah, and the Psalmist is here addressing him in the second person, not speaking of him in the third.”
also loves judgment; thou hast established equity, thou hast done judgment and righteousness in Jacob.
 
1 Jehovah reigns The people, who were formerly called upon to rejoice, are now commanded to tremble. For as the Jews were encompassed by enemies, it was of the utmost importance that God’s power should be magnified among them, that they might know that, while under his guardianship, they would be constantly and completely safe from the hatred and fury of every foe. The Hebrew word רגז, ragaz, as we have elsewhere seen, sometimes signifies to tremble, at other times, to be angry, and, in short, denotes any strong emotion arising either from anger or fear.
רגז, ragaz, “denoting commotion either of the body or mind, imports in the latter acceptation particularly two things, fear and anger, those two principal emotions of the mind. In the sense of anger we have it in Genesis 45:24, where we render it falling out or quarrelling, and in 2 Kings 19:27, 28, where we render it rage So, Proverbs 29:9, and in Genesis 41:10, the Hebrew קצף, (affirmed of Pharaoh, viz., that) he was wroth, is by the Chaldee rendered רגז. And this is much the more frequent acceptation of the word in the Old Testament.” — Hammond’s note on Psalm 4:4. On the text before us, after observing that Abu Walid explains this root as signifying in the Arabic trembling and commotion, arising sometimes from anger, sometimes from fear, and other causes, the same critic says, “Here the context may seem to direct the taking it in the notion of commotion simply, as that signifies ἀκαταστασία, sedition or tumult of rebels or other adversaries. And then the sense will be thus: ‘The Lord reigneth, let the people be moved,’ i e., Now God hath set up David in his throne, and peaceably settled the kingdom in him, in spite of all the commotions of the people. The LXX. render it to this sense, as Psalm 4:4, ὀργιζέσθωσαν, ‘let the people be angry or regret it as much as they will.’” The verb here, and the concluding verb of the verse, may be read in the future tense: “The people or nations shall tremble, and the earth shall be moved,” just as at the giving of the Law, “the people trembled,” and “the earth shook.” Thus the passage may be regarded as a prediction of the subjection of the heathen world to the dominion of Christ.
Accordingly, the prophet here intends that God, in the emancipation of his chosen people, should give such a palpable display of his power, as would strike all the nations with dismay, and make them feel how madly they had rushed upon their own destruction. For it is with regard to men that God is said to reign, when he exalts himself by the magnificent displays which he gives of his power; because, while the aid which he gives to them remains invisible, unbelievers act a more presumptuous part, just as if there were no God.

See <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 6. 23, <ns0:hi>&c. Ioel</ns0:hi> 2. 17.</ns0:note> among them that call upon his name <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who used frequently and solemnly to intercede with God on the behalf of the people. So the general ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression is here used synecdochically for this particular kind of prayer: such Synecdoche's being very frequent in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture.</ns0:note>: they called upon the LORD, and he answered them <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Moses, Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. and elsewhere; <ns0:hi>Aaron, Numb.</ns0:hi> 16. <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 19. and 12. 19. Compare <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 15. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 He spake unto them <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To some of them; for the expression is only in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />definite and therefore doth not necessarily reach to all of them: to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> frequently; to <ns0:hi>Aaron, Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. 24. and 33. 9, 10, 11. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 12. 5. And for <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> he answered him if not by words yet really and by his actions, thundering a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst the Philistins, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 9, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which supposeth a Cloud, if not a Cloudy Pillar.</ns0:note> in the cloudy pillar: they kept his testimonies, and the ordinance <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> he gave them <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This is added not onely for their commendation but for the instruction of the Israelites to teach them that God will not hear the Prayers of them who do not keep his Commandments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Thou answerdest them <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The intercessours beforementioned. Either 1. <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> who did sin, and whose sins God did pardon, yet so as that he did punish them with exclusion from the land of <ns0:hi>Canaan;</ns0:hi> of which see <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 20. 12. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 50, 51. Or rather 2. the people for whom they prayed; which though not expressed may be easily understood from the following words and from the Histories to which these words relate. For this <ns0:hi>forgiving</ns0:hi> was evidently the effect of Gods <ns0:hi>answer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing</ns0:hi> the Prayers of the persons above mentioned. And there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore as their Prayers recorded in Scripture were not for the pardon of their own sins, but for the pardon of the peoples sins, so this forgiveness granted was for the sins of the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple. And whereas the people are not here mentioned; it must be remembred that in Scripture the relative is fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently put without the antecedent, as it is <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 7. 89. and 114. 2. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 14. 26.</ns0:note>, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them <ns0:hi>a,</ns0:hi> though thou tookest vengeance of their inventi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This clause limits and ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plains the former. Thou didst forgive the sins of the people not absolutely and universally, for thou didst punish them se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verely, but so far as not to inflict that total and final destru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction upon them which they deserved, and thou hadst threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 10, 14, 34.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:492" />9 Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy hill <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either in <ns0:hi>Zion:</ns0:hi> or in his Church typified by it, and oft called <ns0:hi>Zion.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: for the LORD our God is holy.</ns0:p>
